events.title: Macintosh 128K released
events.summary: Apple shipped the Macintosh 128K on January 24, 1984 — the first commercially successful mass-market computer with a graphical user interface and mouse at an accessible price.
events.about: The Mac brought windows, menus, and icons to consumers — [HyperCard], MacPaint, and desktop publishing followed. Developers used MPW, Think C, and later CodeWarrior; the [GUI] forced new interaction models that Windows copied. Susan Kare's icons and the "1984" launch defined how non-programmers could use computers.

narrative.whyChosen: The Macintosh made the [GUI] a consumer product, not a lab demo.
narrative.whyImportant: It shifted software design toward visual, direct-manipulation interfaces — still the model for web and mobile [UI].
narrative.problemSolved: Command-line PCs intimidated mainstream users; Apple bet on approachable graphics and a unified design language.

events.title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly first published
events.summary: Emmanuel Goldstein launched 2600: The Hacker Quarterly in January 1984 — a magazine documenting phone [phreaking], BBS culture, and early computer intrusion techniques.
events.about: 2600 became the longest-running print voice of the hacker underground — meetups, HOPE conferences, and legal advocacy alongside exploit write-ups. It bridged phone phreaks and [PC] crackers, preserving techniques that would later surface in Phrack, [DEF CON], and modern bug-bounty culture.

narrative.whyChosen: 2600 is the enduring print institution of American hacker culture.
narrative.whyImportant: It legitimized security research as a community practice outside vendor silos.
narrative.problemSolved: Hackers lacked a durable forum to share techniques and organize outside corporate R&D labs.
